implementation_notes: The pattern is written exactly as it reads: def cancel(self, order_id): return self._repo.cancel(order_id), with @property for the attribute form (return self._inner.name). What replaces repetitive one-liners for a wrapper is __getattr__, which forwards any attribute the class does not define to the wrapped object - convenient for generated proxies, but it hides the real interface and makes hasattr-based feature checks, dir() and IDE completion stop telling the truth, so keep it out of hand-written APIs. A one-liner that must be overridden by subclasses should stay an ordinary def; properties are descriptors and cannot be shadowed by instance attributes without a setter.
pitfalls: __getattr__ forwarding makes every name exist: hasattr, getattr(obj, name, default) and completion stop telling the truth, and typos surface as late runtime failures.

Descriptors live on the class, so a property cannot be shadowed by instance state (self.count = 3 raises unless a setter exists) - the opposite of a plain attribute, which would silently shadow the one-liner.
A one-liner that calls super() relies on the zero-argument form's enclosing-class cell; moving the call into a nested function or comprehension captures the wrong frame and breaks it.
